source.title: Structure tokens sharpen the feature vocabulary of protein language models

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some extracted text has minor formatting artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether descriptions of learned features predict held-out activations, using SAE features in protein language models rather than native neuron poles.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates descriptions generated from top-activating residues against held-out feature activations. These results are relevant to the explanation-prediction aspect of V6 and automated scoring aspect of V7, but the units are SAE features, not native neurons or neuron poles. It does not report the one-job/two-job/unknown shares, and its held-out inputs are protein sequences rather than ordinary text. Other reported interpretability measures, such as GO enrichment, do not measure the claim versions' named outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study scores LLM-written descriptions of sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, not native neurons, in protein models (ESM-2, ESM-3), and cites neither original source. V6 and V7 concern explanations of native neurons in language models. The SAE-feature autointerpretability scores (median r 0.60–0.79) are therefore a related but different construct. They are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests of V6/V7. No result bears on V1–V5 (no neuron-pole audit, no InceptionV1, no vision or tool-scaling estimates, no neuron attribution graphs). T6/cites_only is the nearest category: the study neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The headline conclusions are about SAE features, not neurons, in ESM-2 and ESM-3. 78% of features converge across the two models (null 14.2%), and convergent features carry most functional-site signal. Structure tokens sharpen rather than replace the feature vocabulary. A single head, L0H7, is the bottleneck for structure input. Steering, attribution patching and feature circuits show the features are causally involved. ESM-3 features also get higher autointerpretability scores than ESM-2 features, with strong agreement between the two judges.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse autoencoders to extract protein-model features, generates descriptions from top-activating residues, and scores predictions on held-out proteins; it does not perform a neuron-pole audit.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported median prediction-activation correlation differs between ESM-3 and ESM-2 and between the two judges.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM descriptions of SAE features from top-activating residues predict held-out per-residue activations. Median Pearson r is 0.79/0.75 for ESM-3 and 0.60/0.61 for ESM-2 (Claude/GPT judges). Judges agree on per-feature ranking (r=0.91, 0.90). 7–37% of features yielded no parseable predictions and were excluded.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Simulation-scored explanations of SAE features in protein language models achieve moderate-to-high median held-out correlations, varying by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Extended Data Fig. 4a: in the automated annotation, the majority of SAE features are classified as 'unknown' motif type.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Most protein-model SAE features lack a category assignment under automated annotation.

record.problems: Autointerpretability was evaluated on 300 randomly sampled features per model, and some descriptions lacked parseable predictions and were excluded. The text gives medians but no numerical confidence intervals for these scores and defines no threshold for a good score. The tested units are SAE features rather than native neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported results—including GO enrichment, reconstruction fidelity, functional-site probes, feature convergence, and causal interventions—do not measure neuron-pole job counts or held-out prediction scores for the feature descriptions and were not entered as rows.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or one-job/two-job/unknown shares.
No neuron-level shares in any language model; only SAE features in two protein models.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No test of architecture or tools driving native-neuron interpretability.
No attribution graphs from the model's own neurons. Circuits are built from SAE features, with reconstruction error (cosine 0.98/0.92).
No native-neuron simulation scoring on text, and no share of neurons above a good-score threshold.

missing.what: Share of SAE features classified as unknown by the autointerpretability annotation (majority; exact number not in text). This is relevant only if SAE-feature analogues of V1 shares are tracked.

record.verdict_notes: Units are TopK SAE features (k=64, expansion factor 8), not neurons, in protein models with protein-sequence inputs. The author consults for Anthropic. The record's claim of no CIs conflicts with the Fig. 1 legend. The record's 300 features per model is wrong for ESM-2 (270).

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or neuron-pole job counts.
Only ESM-2 and ESM-3 are studied; feature convergence is not a measurement of the claimed one-job/two-job/unknown shares, and no dense/MoE or trillion-parameter models are tested.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or recursive-generalization analysis.
No vision-model estimates or test of the claimed architecture/tool explanation for messy neurons.
The study examines SAE features and causal interventions, not attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or their reconstruction error.
Tests held-out prediction for SAE feature descriptions in protein models, not explanations of native neuron poles in language-model text settings.
Reports automated held-out scoring of SAE feature descriptions, but not the proportion of native neurons above a defined good-score threshold; inputs are protein sequences, not ordinary text.
